name: Banen (Ndogtuna)
overview: Having come from Ndiki (Mbam) via the West and Makombé, the Banen Ndogtuna found in Yabassi a land of welcome where they live alongside the Bandem, Basaa, Bamiléké, Hausa, Bamoun, Beti, Bodiman and Dibum. Organised in hereditary chiefdoms, they live from farming, fishing and hunting, and celebrate the Ngankam every year in April.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Majority group in a mixed environment (Bandem, Basaa, Bamiléké, Hausa, Bamoun, Beti, Bodiman, Dibum), many of whom also speak Basaa, Duala, Bandem or a Bamiléké language.
The Banen speech variety is found in Penja, Loum, Douala and Ndiki.
Marriages take place mostly within the group, even though men often take a wife from outside.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: Yabassi is a land of welcome, with no particular religious significance.
The group comes from Ndiki (Nemeki), with stopovers in the West and at Makombé; ties with these places are maintained.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: Sociopolitical life rests on hereditary chiefdoms; decisions fall to the village chief.
Relations between notables, chief and population are good.
Cohabitation outside marriage and marriage between relatives by marriage are forbidden; the wife owes respect to her husband.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship; the girl leaves her family to join her husband.
Circumcision marks the boy's entry into manhood; puberty makes the girl a woman ready to marry.
Ages given today: 21 for the man, 18 for the woman.
Formerly, the father chose his son's wife, and abduction existed; today, all the steps are followed (“knocking” at the door, request, bride price).
Bride price gifts: kola nuts, avocados, wrapper, salt, cod, rice, tobacco, red oil, machete. The avocado is meant to make the child strong, the machete is for cultivating the fields.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: The ngambi cult (divination by the spider) is practised when needed by a healer, in the forest or at home.
Birth and death are natural phenomena; death can also be a divine punishment.
One joins the dead during certain ceremonies or by meditating at the graves.
Taboos: witchcraft, incest, murder, infidelity. One does not take one's brother's wife or anyone else's.
Murder is the first of the prohibitions; serious offences are punished by public beating, banishment or quarantine.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Men: farming, fishing, hunting. Women: farming, fishing, home.
The land goes first to the first occupants, then to the communities that live on it.
Ancestral basketry crafts: mats, baskets, hampers (mintɛtɛ).

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Men wear the wrapper, women the kaba ŋgondo.
Traditional medicine is widely used to treat many illnesses.
Beauty: the strong, hard-working man, a good warrior; the strong and beautiful woman, formerly marked with scarification on the face.
Courtship: the man hard-working and strong, the woman with good manners.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Rhythms: minkumkum, naka naka and mút, to the sound of the tam-tam and the drum.
The minkumkum, a men's dance, honours a deceased person; the naka naka is danced by women; the mút pays tribute to a late father of a family.
Community festival: the Ngankam, every year in April.

sections.title: The names
items: No general structure, except for twins (e.g. Esome).
The name is given without ceremony and does not change.
One avoids calling someone by his or her own name (for example, one says “Olé”); the appellative a- replaces the prefix: à-Manja.
The founding ancestor is called Bisoum.

lessons.title: Who are the Banen (Ndogtuna)? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Banen (Ndogtuna) community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Banen (Ndogtuna) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Banen (Ndogtuna) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Banen (Ndogtuna) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Banen (Ndogtuna) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Banen (Ndogtuna) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Group in the majority in a mixed environment (Bandem, Basaa, Bamiléké, Haoussa, Bamoun, Beti, Bodiman, Dibum), many of whom also speak Basaa, Duala, Bandem or a Bamiléké language. • The Banen speech variety is also found at Penja, Loum, Douala and Ndiki. • Marriages take place mostly within the group, even though men often take wives from outside. • Yabassi is a land of welcome, with no particular religious significance. • The group comes from Ndiki (Nemeki), with stages in the West and at Makombé; ties with these places are maintained.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Having come from Ndiki (Mbam) via the West and Makombé, the Banen Ndogtuna found in Yabassi a land of welcome where they live alongside the Bandem, Basaa, Bamiléké, Hausa, Bamoun, Beti, Bodiman and Dibum. Organised in hereditary chiefdoms, they live from farming, fishing and hunting, and celebrate the Ngankam every year in April.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Banen (Ndogtuna) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Power and social organisation among the Banen (Ndogtuna)
lessons.anelcac: Socio-political organisation, rules for living together
lessons.competence: Describe how the Banen (Ndogtuna) organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.
lessons.situation: An important decision must be made for the whole Banen (Ndogtuna) village. Who decides, and how?
lessons.materiel: The community's cultural profile, paper and felt-tip pens for the organisation chart.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “An important decision has to be made for the whole Banen (Ndogtuna) village. Who decides, and how?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.instruction: Draw a diagram (organisation chart) of power among the Banen (Ndogtuna), then explain in 3 sentences how a decision is made.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)

lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Banen (Ndogtuna)
objectives: Linking food to the living environment
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Banen (Ndogtuna), describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.

lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Banen (Ndogtuna), describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Banen (Ndogtuna).” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: cassava, macabo, taro, couscous, njamba sauce (cassava leaves). • Drinks: palm wine. • Men: farming, fishing, hunting. Women: farming, fishing, home.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Banen (Ndogtuna) mainly eat cassava, macabo, taro, couscous, njamba sauce. Traditional drinks: palm wine. These dishes are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

lessons.title: Birth, name and the passage to adulthood among the Banen (Ndogtuna)
objectives: Explain the meaning of a birth

lessons.competence: Explain how the Banen (Ndogtuna) welcome a child, give the child a name and mark the child's entry into adulthood.
lessons.situation: A child has just been born in a Banen (Ndogtuna) family. How will he be named, and how will he become an adult?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain how the Banen (Ndogtuna) welcome a child, give it a name and mark its entry into adulthood.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What does a birth mean for the community? — Who gives the name, when and how? — Can the name change during a lifetime? — When and how does one become a man or a woman?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)

activities.title: I describe
activities.instruction: Choose the most representative dance: participants, instruments, attire, gestures.

activities.title: I understand
activities.instruction: Explain whether it is a dance of joy, mourning, initiation or war.

activities.title: I practise
activities.instruction: With your group, act out the dance in front of the class.

student.memo: Among the Banen (Ndogtuna), traditional dances (men, tribute to the deceased, naka naka, tribute to the father of the family) accompany the great moments of life: celebrations, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: tam-tam, drum. Festival(s): Ngankam.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Banen (Ndogtuna)
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Banen (Ndogtuna), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Banen (Ndogtuna). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Banen (Ndogtuna), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Banen (Ndogtuna). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • Men: farming, fishing, hunting. Women: farming, fishing, home. • Land goes first to the first occupants, then to the communities that live on it. • Ancestral basketry crafts: mats, baskets, hampers (mintɛtɛ).

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Men: farming, fishing, hunting. Women: farming, fishing, home. Land goes first to the first occupants, then to the communities that live on it.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a two-column table (men / women) of the Banen (Ndogtuna)'s activities, then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Discover how the Banen (Ndogtuna) make a living from their work.

activities.title: I classify
activities.instruction: Classify the activities in a men / women table.

activities.title: I explain
activities.instruction: Explain how one obtains land to cultivate.

activities.title: I calculate
activities.instruction: Imagine the calendar of a working year (seasons, harvests, festivals).

activities.title: I propose
activities.instruction: Suggest a project idea that promotes a local skill.

student.memo: Men: farming, fishing, hunting. Women: farming, fishing, home. Land goes first to the first occupants, then to the communities that live on it.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Banen (Ndogtuna)
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death
lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Banen (Ndogtuna), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Banen (Ndogtuna). Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Banen (Ndogtuna), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Banen (Ndogtuna). Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The ngambi cult (divination by spider) is practised when needed by a healer, in the forest or at home. • Birth and death are natural phenomena; death may also be a divine punishment. • One joins the dead during certain ceremonies or by meditating at the graves. • Taboos: witchcraft, incest, murder, infidelity. One does not take one's brother's wife or anyone else's. • Murder is the first of the prohibitions; serious offences are punished by public flogging, banishment or quarantine.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The ngambi cult (divination by the spider) is practised when needed by a healer, in the forest or at home. Birth and death are natural phenomena; death can also be a divine punishment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Banen (Ndogtuna) (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Discover what the Banen (Ndogtuna) believe, the places they respect and the taboos they observe.

activities.title: I identify
activities.instruction: Identify two sacred places and what they recall.

activities.title: I explain
activities.instruction: Explain the usefulness of a taboo for the life of the group.

activities.title: I show respect
activities.instruction: Write the guide for the respectful visitor.

activities.title: I compare
activities.instruction: Compare with a taboo you know in your family.

student.memo: The ngambi cult (divination by the spider) is practised when needed by a healer, in the forest or at home. Birth and death are natural phenomena; death can also be a divine punishment.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Tunen
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day

vocabulary.frenchText: morning greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Banen (Ndogtuna) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Banen (Ndogtuna) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Banen (Ndogtuna) greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Banen (Ndogtuna) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The community's language is Tunen. • Greetings: Wàyáâ = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); wàyésíì = morning greeting (one person); Ànûwà yáâ = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Bəmbɔt, Bəfan, Bəlaa, Binis, Bəlan. • The founding ancestor is called Bisoum.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Tunen are the first steps towards communicating with the Banen (Ndogtuna). Polite formulas express the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Learn to greet, introduce yourself and count in Tunen.

activities.title: I greet
activities.instruction: Learn the greeting formulas for morning, midday and evening.

activities.title: I introduce myself
activities.instruction: Say your name, where you are from and where you live.

activities.title: I count
activities.instruction: Count objects from 1 to 10.

activities.title: I pass on
activities.instruction: Teach a formula to a classmate or a family member.

student.memo: Greeting and counting in Tunen are the first steps towards communicating with the Banen (Ndogtuna). Polite formulas express the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.
